古箏主要用於中國古典音樂與民間音樂，並分山東、河南、潮州、客家、浙江等地方樂派；: The guzheng is used mainly in Chinese classical and folk music, and falls into regional schools such as Shandong, Henan, Chaozhou, Hakka and Zhejiang; listen to pieces such as "High Mountains and Flowing Water", "Autumn Moon over the Han Palace", "Cold Crows at Play in the Water", "Lotus Emerging from the Water" and "The General's Command". New works such as "Spring Dawn on the Snowy Mountains" and "Battling the Typhoon" appeared after the 1950s, and experimental works such as "Bright Mountain" and "Hidden Fragrance" after the 1980s, along with collaborations with electronics, jazz and orchestras.
古箏為中國撥弦樂器。來源稱其起源有多說：或謂早期似箏樂器由秦將蒙恬受瑟影響創製；: The guzheng is a Chinese plucked instrument. The source says its origin is disputed: one account has an early zither-like instrument created by the Qin general Meng Tian under the influence of the se; another has it first made as a bamboo-tube zheng, recorded in the Shuowen Jiezi, and later changed to a large curved wooden board with movable bridges; a third tells of two men quarrelling over a se and splitting it into twelve and thirteen strings. The earliest known surviving example has thirteen strings and may belong to the Warring States period. It flourished in the Qin dynasty and was perhaps most common in the Tang. It gave rise to the Japanese koto, the Korean gayageum and ajaeng, the Mongolian yatga and the Vietnamese đàn tranh. String material changed from silk to brass wire, and from the 1970s mostly steel-core nylon; 21, 25 and 26 strings are common today.
古箏為撥弦齊特琴，以泡桐共鳴面板與可移動琴柱支撐弦，音色輕亮，音域寬廣。高音弦靠: The guzheng is a plucked zither whose strings are carried over a paulownia soundboard and movable bridges; its timbre is light and bright and its range wide. The high strings are nearest the player and the low strings on the far side, and nylon, steel or silk strings may be used according to repertoire; modern steel-core nylon strings add volume while the timbre remains acceptable. The two notes outside the pentatonic scale are obtained by pressing the strings, and left-hand slides and vibrato and rapid thumb work in the right hand can change the dynamics, while striking can be hard or soft. Unlike the guqin, the guzheng has movable bridges; it is also the ancestor of Asian zither-type instruments such as the Japanese koto and the Korean gayageum.

The strings may be nylon, steel or silk according to style; modern strings are mostly steel core wrapped in nylon, while in the Qing period brass and other metal wire came into use. The plectra worn on the fingers may be plastic, resin, tortoiseshell or ivory, and in earlier times bamboo, bone, animal tooth and jade were also used. Decoration of the body includes carved lacquer, straw, mother-of-pearl, carved shell and cloisonné; materials the source does not state are not supplied.

The guzheng (zheng) is a Chinese plucked zither, Hornbostel–Sachs 312.22-5. Modern instruments commonly have 21, 25 or 26 strings and are about 1.6 metres long, sounding through a large paulownia soundboard, with other parts mostly of other woods. The strings may be nylon, steel or silk according to style, and are usually tuned to a major pentatonic scale; the high strings are nearest the player and the low strings on the far side. It is played by plucking with the fingers or with nail picks, the left hand pressing the strings for slides and vibrato. It is found throughout China and is used in Chinese classical music, traditional styles and modern composition.

演奏古箏時，高音弦靠近演奏者，低音弦在另一側；弦序由內至外為1至21。發聲以手指: In playing the guzheng the high strings are nearest the player and the low strings on the far side; the strings are numbered 1 to 21 from the inner side outwards. Sound is made by plucking with the fingers, with plectra of plastic, resin, tortoiseshell or ivory, in modern practice usually fixed to up to four fingers of each hand. In the traditional method the right hand plucks and the left hand presses the strings to the left of the movable bridges for slides and vibrato; in modern practice both hands play to the right of the strings. A beginner should first learn the order of the strings and the pentatonic scale, then practise right-hand plucking and left-hand stopping as ornament.
